medium.conteudo_html:
It is Tuesday afternoon. You have a proposal due tomorrow, a pile of notes from three different calls, and a colleague waiting on your feedback.

You open Claude, type “help me with my proposal,” and get back a polite, generic answer that could apply to anyone, anywhere.

That is not Claude’s fault. “Help me with my proposal” is not a task. It is a wish. Claude is very good at long documents, careful reasoning, and nuanced writing, but it can only work with what you hand it.

This guide shares practical Claude prompts for work that give it something real to work with. You will see why they work, how to adapt them, and how to build a small personal library so you stop starting from a blank box every time.

Why Claude Rewards Clear Prompts

Claude tends to shine when the job involves reading a lot, thinking carefully, and writing in a natural tone. That makes it a strong fit for everyday knowledge work: summarizing, drafting, editing, planning, and weighing options.

But the quality of what comes back depends on the quality of what goes in. Think of Claude as a sharp colleague who just joined your team today. They are capable, but they do not know your audience, your deadline, or your standards. Tell them, and they get to work.

A good prompt does three things:

  • It removes guesswork so Claude does not have to assume what you meant.
  • It saves revision rounds because the first draft lands closer to the target.
  • It becomes reusable, so a prompt that worked on Monday works again on Friday.

Here is a simple frame you can keep in your head:

Role + Task + Context + Format + Constraints

For example: “You are an editor (role). Tighten this report (task). It is for busy executives who skim (context). Give me the revised version plus a three-bullet list of changes (format). Keep it under 400 words (constraints).”

If you would like to see well-built prompts before writing your own, you can download the free prompt collection and try a few on your own work today.

Mistakes That Waste Claude’s Strengths

Before the prompts, here are the habits that quietly drain value.

Being vague about the reader. “Write an update” could be for your boss, your team, or a client. Each needs a different tone. Name the reader.

Pasting nothing. Claude handles long documents well. If you want feedback on a draft, paste the draft. Describing it in a sentence throws away its biggest advantage.

Skipping the format. If you want a table, a short email, or five bullets, say so. Otherwise you will get whatever Claude guesses is best.

Accepting the first answer as final. Treat the response as a draft. Follow up with “shorter,” “warmer,” “more direct,” or “explain your reasoning.” Claude is built for this back-and-forth.

Hiding the constraints. Word limits, deadlines, brand voice, and things to avoid all belong in the prompt.

Claude Prompts for Writing and Editing

Writing is where many people first feel the benefit. These prompts keep your voice while cutting the grind.

The first-draft starter

I need to write [type of document] for [audience]. The goal is [goal]. Key points to cover: [list]. Tone: [tone]. Length: about [number] words. Write a first draft and mark any place where you had to guess a fact so I can check it.

That last sentence matters. Asking Claude to flag its own guesses makes fact-checking faster.

The ruthless editor

Edit the text below for clarity and concision. Keep my voice and meaning. Remove filler, fix awkward sentences, and tell me the three biggest changes you made and why. [paste text]

The tone adjuster

Rewrite this message so it sounds friendly but professional. Keep it under 120 words and keep every deadline unchanged. [paste message]

The structure check

Read this draft and tell me, without rewriting it, where the argument is weakest, where I am repeating myself, and what a skeptical reader would question first. [paste draft]

Notice that this one asks for feedback only. Telling Claude not to rewrite keeps you in control of your own words.

Claude Prompts for Reading, Research, and Summaries

Claude’s ability to digest long text is one of its most practical strengths.

The executive summary

Summarize the document below for a busy executive. Give me: a two-sentence overview, five key points, any risks or open questions, and recommended next steps. [paste document]

The “explain it to me” prompt

Explain [topic] as if I am smart but new to the field. Use one real-world analogy, define any jargon the first time it appears, and end with three questions I should ask an expert.

The comparison builder

Compare [option A] and [option B] for [my situation]. Put the result in a table covering cost, effort, risk, and long-term fit. Then give a short recommendation and say what would change your mind.

Asking “what would change your mind” is a handy trick. It surfaces the assumptions behind the recommendation, which helps you decide whether they apply to you.

The notes cleaner

Turn these rough notes into a clean summary with decisions made, action items, owners, and deadlines. If anything is unclear, list it separately as a question. [paste notes]

Claude Prompts for Planning and Decisions

Planning prompts work best when you are honest about limits.

The realistic day plan

Here are my tasks: [list]. I have [number] hours of focused time, meetings at [times], and my energy is best in the [morning/afternoon]. Order the tasks, tell me what to postpone, and keep the plan realistic rather than ambitious.

The weekly reset

Help me plan next week. My goals: [list]. Fixed commitments: [list]. Suggest a simple rhythm, name the three tasks that matter most, and point out any conflicts you notice.

The decision partner

I am deciding whether to [decision]. Here is what I know: [facts]. Here is what worries me: [concerns]. Lay out the strongest case for each side, then ask me three questions that would help me decide.

This is a good example of using Claude to think with you rather than for you. You still make the call, but you make it with a clearer view.

The pre-mortem

Imagine this project failed six months from now: [describe project]. List the five most likely reasons, rank them by probability, and suggest one small action now to reduce each risk.

Claude Prompts for Communication and Admin

Admin work is small tasks stacked up, and prompts shrink it nicely.

The email triage prompt

Here are my recent emails: [paste]. Sort them into reply today, reply this week, and no reply needed. Draft a short reply for the urgent ones.

The polite decline

Write a kind message declining this request because I do not have capacity. Offer one alternative if there is a sensible one. Keep it under 80 words.

The feedback giver

I need to give feedback to a colleague about [situation]. Help me write it so it is specific, kind, and focused on behavior rather than personality. Include one suggested next step.

The meeting prep prompt

I have a meeting about [topic] with [people]. My goal is [goal]. Create a short agenda, three questions I should ask, and two objections I should be ready for.

Examples Across Different Kinds of Work

Every role has its own friction. Here are adaptable prompts for a few common ones.

Marketing:

I have one hour to prepare this week’s content. Suggest a workflow that gets three posts drafted, edited, and ready to schedule in that time.

Sales and client work:

Here is a client’s last email and my notes from our call: [paste]. Draft a follow-up that summarizes what we agreed, confirms next steps, and keeps the tone warm.

Coding and technical work:

Here is a function and the error it throws: [paste]. Explain in plain language what is going wrong, suggest a fix, and tell me how to test it.

Teaching and training:

Create a 45-minute lesson plan on [topic] for [level]. Include a warm-up, a main activity, a check for understanding, and a short take-home task.

Management:

Here are my team’s current projects and deadlines: [list]. Flag where people may be overloaded and suggest one change to balance the workload.

Learning something new:

I want to learn [skill] in 30 days with 25 minutes a day. Build a daily plan with a small practice task and a weekly check-in question.

Each example names a goal, a reader or situation, and a limit. That is the pattern worth copying.

Looking for more ideas you can adapt like these? The free prompt collection is a simple way to explore different styles and find the ones that suit your work.

A Quick Before-and-After

Before:

Help me with my proposal.

You will probably get a general outline that fits nobody in particular.

After:

I run a small design studio and I am writing a proposal for a local restaurant group that wants a full rebrand. The reader is the owner, who is not technical and cares most about cost and timeline. Below are my notes from our call. Write a one-page proposal with an overview, scope, timeline, and pricing section. Keep the tone confident and warm, avoid jargon, and flag anything where my notes are unclear. [paste notes]

The second version tells Claude who is reading, what they care about, what to produce, and how to behave when information is missing. The result is something you can send after a quick polish.

Building a Simple Claude Workflow

The real gain is not one great prompt. It is a routine.

Here is a lightweight version:

  1. Start of day (5 minutes): Paste your task list into your planning prompt and get a realistic order.
  2. During the day: Use your writing, summary, and email prompts as needed instead of improvising each time.
  3. Before meetings (3 minutes): Run your meeting prep prompt.
  4. End of day (3 minutes): Paste what you finished and ask for a short recap plus tomorrow’s top three.
  5. Weekly (10 minutes): Run your weekly reset and note what to change.

Keep your best prompts in one document, with brackets where the details change. After two weeks you will have a personal toolkit that fits how you actually work.

If you would rather start with a bigger organized set instead of building everything yourself, the premium prompt collection offers extra depth across common tasks, so you are not creating each prompt from scratch.

Tips for Better Results Every Time

  • Paste the real material. Drafts, notes, and data beat descriptions.
  • Say who the reader is. Audience changes tone, length, and detail.
  • Ask for reasoning when it matters. “Explain why you chose this” helps you spot weak assumptions.
  • Ask what is missing. “What information would make this answer better?” often reveals a gap.
  • Iterate in small steps. One change per follow-up keeps results predictable.
  • Check facts and numbers. Claude can be wrong, so verify anything that matters before you rely on it.
  • Protect private information. Avoid pasting sensitive personal, financial, or client details, and follow your workplace rules.
  • Stay in charge. Claude suggests. You decide.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are Claude prompts different from ChatGPT prompts? The basic structure is the same: role, task, context, format, constraints. Most good prompts work across different AI tools with small tweaks, so a library you build is rarely wasted.

How long should a prompt be? As long as it needs to be. A few clear sentences with real context usually beat a single vague line, and a long pasted document is fine when it is relevant.

Can I use Claude for sensitive work documents? Be careful. Follow your organization’s policies and avoid sharing confidential details unless you are sure it is allowed.

What if the answer is not quite right? Do not start over. Tell Claude what to change: shorter, more direct, a different audience, a clearer structure. Small corrections often fix it quickly.

How many prompts do I actually need? Most people get a lot of value from five to ten reliable prompts for their regular tasks. Start small and add more only when you notice a repeated need.

Final Thoughts

Working well with Claude is not about secret phrases. It is about giving clear information, asking for a usable format, and saving what works.

Pick one prompt from this post, try it on something you are working on today, and see how the result compares to what you would have written alone. If it helps, save it. If not, change one detail and try again.

When you are ready for more, explore the free prompt collection for extra ideas, or look at the premium collection if you want a larger library ready to use.

medium.titulo: I built my own AI dev tool for under $100. You shouldn’t care (to some extent)
medium.resumo: Open X or Reddit on any given day and someone is showing off a new tool for AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, and pi, which…
medium.conteudo_html:
Open X or Reddit on any given day and someone is showing off a new tool for AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, and pi, which write and change code on a developer’s behalf. There are enough of these tools that people keep lists. awesome-agent-orchestrators started in January 2026 and already tracks 239 projects. They’re shiny and open source, and most of them cost more to adopt than they’re worth. Adopting one means changing how a team works to suit the tool, when an agent can now build one that fits the team in a few hours for less than $100. I just built my own, an orchestrator that runs several coding agents side by side, and you shouldn’t care about mine either.

The payback maths changed

Working around a tool that wasn’t built for the way a team works still costs a lot, and so does living without the automations nobody found the time to write. The webcomic xkcd put numbers on that second cost years ago, in a chart that works as a payback table. Shave five minutes off something you do every day, and you can spend six days automating it before you come out behind over five years. For most teams, six days of a developer’s time was a hard sell for an internal tool, so people kept doing the task by hand. When an AI agent writes the tool in an afternoon, shaving 30 seconds off a daily task already pays for it.

Open source is Pinterest for geeks

Open source used to be cool. You’d browse GitHub, find something interesting, and start using it the same day.

It used to save time as well (anyone who has lost a weekend to their Linux setup would disagree). Instead of writing software yourself, you picked it up from other enthusiasts, joined the discussion, and nudged the direction it took.

For most projects that isn’t true any more. GitHub has turned into a cemetery of projects that work and that nobody looks after, and for a business, adopting one of them is a risk. Nobody fixes it when it breaks or decides where it goes next, and the team loses more time than it ever saved. Even the orchestrator list above has a “Resting” section for projects with no new code in the last few months, and 16 of its 239 are already in it.

There are exceptions, and they’re usually led by people the community already follows. T3 Code and herdr both manage coding agents, and OpenClaw is an AI assistant that runs on your own computer.

The ideas people publish are still precious, though. One person finds a neat way of working with Claude. Another comes up with running pi inside tmux, which keeps several terminal sessions open in one window, and a third tries a different way of reading the changes an agent made. You pin the ones you like, the way you would on Pinterest, and later build your own version.

My own orchestrator took a few hours to build

I needed an orchestrator for pi, and none of the ones out there worked for me. So I pointed Claude at herdr, the Ghostty terminal, and pi (along with its plugins) and told it to build one for me. It took a few hours and a stack of plan documents that I reviewed, it cost less than $100, and it worked as expected on the first try. What I asked for was specific to how I work:

  • keyboard-first navigation, so I can move between agents without reaching for the mouse
  • compatibility with pi, the coding agent I already use
  • a review step in Hunk, a tool built for checking code that agents write
  • a project picker to switch between codebases
  • native git worktree integration, on by default, with a way to opt out
  • keyboard shortcuts I already know from the Warp terminal and Ghostty
  • one prompt that starts many agents at once, such as “Create a new pi session for each GitHub issue”

The orchestrator: agents on the left, a pi session in the middle, Hunk’s review view on the right

If there’s anything I don’t like, I ask Claude to change it. The change goes into the code itself, with the tests written first, and it’s tuned for me and nobody else. Bug fixes go through Claude too, since I’m the only one maintaining the tool, and I review what Claude writes before I rely on it. Claude also writes the documentation as it goes, so a colleague or another agent could pick the tool up while I’m away.

Is it innovative? Maybe, maybe not. There’s a chance someone out there built something that matches my approach 95% of the way, but why give up the other 5% when building my own cost less than $100? Pi is built on the same idea, and its homepage tells users to “Adapt Pi to your workflows, not the other way around.”

Adopt it, fork it, or build your own

Open source is still worth a lot. Adopting someone else’s tool versus building your own is a bit like running Windows versus running Linux. One you take as shipped, the other you reshape until it fits. Adopt when the tool is looked after and nobody on the team has to bend to fit it. Plenty of teams do bend, though, and lose minutes or hours every week working the way some tool’s author decided they should, when they could build their own.

Fork when a tool gets you most of the way and its maintainers have said no to the rest. Forking means taking your own copy of the project and changing it however you like, so it’s building your own with a head start. Maintainers point you that way themselves. In a July 2026 interview, Ghostty’s creator Mitchell Hashimoto said that if you want Ghostty to work differently from how he built it, “just fork and maintain it yourself. That’s not asking any more of you than you’re asking of me.” T3 Code’s project page says it is (mostly) not accepting contributions yet and that big features will not be. Pi automatically closes issues and proposed changes from new contributors by default, and its maintainers reopen the issues worth keeping.

Keeping a personal fork in step with the original project is usually the expensive part of forking. Once an agent handles that, developers get cheap forks and authors no longer have to support everyone’s ideas, which suits both sides.

Build when the workflow is specific to your team and the tool is small enough for an agent to write in an afternoon. That’s where my orchestrator sits, since nobody else works quite the way I do.

So before your team adopts the next tool, work out what building your own would cost. Then go on and prompt. Create your own coding agent, your own orchestrator, or even your own terminal. Just keep saving time in mind the whole way through, or you’ll end up with one more orchestrator to show off on X, and nobody should care about that one either.

medium.resumo: Derive values with computed, react to changes with watch.
medium.conteudo_html:
Derive values with computed, react to changes with watch.

Both respond to reactive changes, but they answer different questions. Mixing them up leads to clunky code.

computed — derive a new value

Use it when a value is calculated from other state. It’s cached and only re-runs when its dependencies change.

import { ref, computed } from 'vue'
const first = ref('Ada')
const last = ref('Lovelace')
const fullName = computed(() => `${first.value} ${last.value}`)
console.log(fullName.value) // "Ada Lovelace"

watch — run a side effect

Use it when a change should trigger an action — fetching data, logging, syncing to storage.

import { ref, watch } from 'vue'
const query = ref('')
watch(query, (newVal, oldVal) => {
  console.log(`searching for ${newVal}`)
  // fetchResults(newVal)
})

The rule of thumb

Returning a value for the template? → computed
Performing an action in response to a change? → watch

If you find yourself manually assigning to a ref inside a watch just to derive a value, you probably want computed instead.

TL;DR: computed produces a cached derived value; watch runs side effects when something changes.

Next time you reach for watch, ask “am I just calculating something?” — if so, computed is cleaner.

medium.titulo: Why I Didn’t Pick the Most Popular Framework for My Game Site
medium.resumo: I built the same MVP with Next.js 14 and Vue 3 + Vite. Three days later, I realized the framework wasn’t the real decision at all.
medium.conteudo_html:
I built the same MVP with Next.js 14 and Vue 3 + Vite. Three days later, I realized the framework wasn’t the real decision at all.

Before I started building my game collection site, I spent a long time agonizing over the tech stack.

Next.js 14 is the popular choice right now. App Router + SSG looks perfect for a content site. Vue 3 + Vite is known for being lightweight — smaller first-load JS, faster builds. Both have good arguments. There are plenty of comparison articles online, but reading them only made me more indecisive. They all compared specs, but none of them told me how to choose given my constraints.

So I stopped reading and started building. Same MVP, two stacks, one after the other. Let the data decide.

What I found was something more important than the stack itself.

What I Actually Cared About

Most people start tech selection by comparing feature lists. But feature lists are infinite. What actually constrains you are just a few things. I wrote down three hard constraints:

One: SEO had to work. Most traffic for a game site comes from search engines. Game detail pages must be crawlable. This wasn’t “nice to have” — it was mandatory.

Two: First load had to be fast. LCP under 2.5s on mobile 4G. Users have only a few seconds of patience. Slow means gone.

Three: The game iframe couldn’t block the main thread. While browsing the list page, no game runtime code should load. I’ll come back to this point, because it turned out to be the real key.

These three constraints ended up driving my entire decision.

Day 1: Next.js Version — Static Export Taught Me a Lesson

I built the homepage, category pages, and game runtime page with Next.js 14 App Router, using output: 'export' for pure static export, deployed to Vercel.

Homepage and category pages generated HTML correctly. But /play/[id] all returned 404.

After digging in: App Router with output: 'export' doesn’t support dynamic routes by default unless you explicitly define generateStaticParams. This is heavily discussed in the community; developers have reported that “the latest Next.js App Router doesn’t support dynamic routes with static generation.”

Worse, even after defining generateStaticParams, all game IDs have to be pre-generated at build time. If the game count grows to hundreds, every new game triggers a full rebuild, and CI time grows exponentially.

I tried @falsefoundation/next-dynamic-exports, which supports dynamic routes by generating fallback pages, but it requires web server rewrite rules, adding deployment complexity.

Then I tried a different approach: turn the game runtime page from a dynamic route into a client-rendered static shell — the /play page reads the game ID via useSearchParams after loading. This bypasses the generateStaticParams limitation, but the game runtime page is no longer prerendered, so SEO suffers. My trade-off: the game runtime page has low SEO value anyway (users arrive from the detail page), so it’s acceptable.

Next.js version data: Homepage LCP 1.2s (mobile 4G throttling), first-load JS ~85KB (gzip), build time 12s.

（When publishing to Medium, embed the code snippets above via Gist to avoid formatting issues. Same for the rest of this article.）

Day 2: Vue 3 + Vite Version — Genuinely Lightweight

Vue’s dev experience was excellent. Vite cold start under 1 second, hot updates nearly imperceptible, build time only 6 seconds — half of Next.js. First-load JS ~50KB, nearly 40% less.

But SEO became a problem.

Vue + Vite defaults to SPA. The homepage and category pages only contain <div id="app"></div> in the HTML — crawlers see no content. The solution was to install vite-plugin-seo-prerender, which prerenders the SPA into static HTML files at build time.

Configuration is simple:

// vite.config.ts
import seoPrerender from 'vite-plugin-seo-prerender'

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    seoPrerender({
      routes: ['/', '/games/puzzle', '/games/sports']
    })
  ]
})

But the plugin has a limitation: it’s only suitable for generating static HTML for a small number of pages. If the game count grows to hundreds, every game detail page needs prerendering, and build time becomes uncontrollable.

Another option is Nuxt 3, Vue’s meta-framework with built-in SSG. But that introduces another framework, contradicting the “lightweight” goal.

Vue version data: Homepage LCP 1.5s (after prerendering), first-load JS ~50KB (gzip), build time 6s.

Day 3: A Counterintuitive Finding

After both versions were running, I did one thing: recorded the full timeline from homepage to clicking “Start Game” using Chrome DevTools Performance panel on both.

Something counterintuitive came up: the performance difference between the two versions was far smaller than I expected.

The Next.js version had 35KB more first-load JS, but on 4G that’s about 200ms of download time. The real time sink while browsing the list page wasn’t the framework’s JS size — it was the game iframe initialization.

In the default implementation, the iframe was initialized when the game detail page mounted. Even if the iframe src pointed to an empty placeholder page, creating the contentWindow and initializing the sandbox environment still consumed main thread time. On a Moto G Power, that single operation took about 400ms.

The correct approach is the facade pattern: render only a lightweight static placeholder (thumbnail + play button) before the iframe mounts, and inject the actual iframe only when the user clicks “Start.” This matches Lighthouse’s recommendation for deferring third-party resources.

There’s a Next.js static wiki case in the DEV community that uses the facade pattern to move a YouTube iframe from hydration-time mount to click-time load, bringing mobile TBT down from destructive levels to acceptable.

This means: the framework choice’s impact on first-load performance is far smaller than the iframe initialization strategy’s impact.

I wrote this down because it directly changed my selection criteria. Before, I was comparing “whose first-load JS is smaller.” Now I was comparing “who makes the facade pattern easier to implement.”

Final Choice: Hybrid Architecture

Based on the three-day comparison, I made these decisions:

Static content pages (homepage, category pages, detail pages) use Next.js SSG.SEO works out of the box, no extra plugins. Dynamic routes have limitations, but the game detail page ID count is manageable (only 6 games initially). If the game count grows to 200+, a Headless CMS with ISR can be introduced, but that requires a server and breaks the zero-backend constraint.

The game runtime page uses an independent client-rendered shell. The game runtime page has low SEO value and doesn’t need prerendering. Use next/dynamicwith ssr: false to lazy-load the game iframe component, facade pattern: initialize the iframe only after the user clicks “Start.”

Here’s the concrete implementation:

// components/GameLauncher.tsx
'use client'
import { useState } from 'react'
import dynamic from 'next/dynamic'

const GameIframe = dynamic(() => import('./GameIframe'), {
  ssr: false,
  loading: () => <div className="h-full bg-zinc-900 animate-pulse" />
})

export default function GameLauncher({ game }) {
  const [started, setStarted] = useState(false)

  if (!started) {
    return (
      <button
        onClick={() => setStarted(true)}
        className="relative w-full aspect-video rounded-lg overflow-hidden"
      >
        <img src={game.thumbnail} alt={game.title} className="w-full h-full object-cover" />
        <div className="absolute inset-0 flex items-center justify-center">
          <svg width="64" height="64" viewBox="0 0 64 64">
            <circle cx="32" cy="32" r="30" fill="rgba(0,0,0,0.6)" />
            <polygon points="26,20 26,44 46,32" fill="white" />
          </svg>
        </div>
      </button>
    )
  }

  return <GameIframe src={game.entry} gameId={game.id} />
}

ssr: false ensures the iframe component isn’t bundled into the HTML during server rendering, and only loads from the client after the user clicks. This matches Next.js’s official lazy-loading advice: for heavy components that don’t participate in SSR, use next/dynamic with ssr: false to reduce the initial bundle.

The Vue version wasn’t maintained. It builds faster and has a smaller bundle, but SEO needs extra plugins, and if the game count grows, the prerendering solution’s scalability is worse than Next.js’s SSG system.

Data Comparison

MetricNext.js 14Vue 3 + ViteFirst-load JS (gzip)~85KB~50KBHomepage LCP (4G)1.2s1.5s (after prerendering)Build time12s6sDynamic route supportNeeds generateStaticParamsBuilt-inSEOOut of the boxNeeds extra pluginsGame runtime lazy loadnext/dynamic native supportManual implementation

Test conditions: MacBook Pro M1 build, iPhone 12 + Chrome DevTools 4G throttling, 10 runs each, median.

Note a counterintuitive result: Vue’s LCP was actually slower than Next.js after prerendering. The reason is that vite-plugin-seo-prerender still includes the full Vue runtime in the generated HTML, while Next.js SSG outputs cleaner HTML with lower hydration cost. This shows that “smaller first-load JS” doesn’t equal “faster first load.”

（When publishing to Medium, turn this table into an image, since Medium doesn’t handle Markdown tables well.）

Trade-offs

Next.js build time is longer. 12s vs 6s. Every new game requires a rebuild. If the game count reaches 50, build time could exceed 30 seconds.

The Vue version was abandoned. It has better dev experience and a smaller bundle, but needs extra work on SEO and scalability. If your game site doesn’t need SEO — an internal tool or pure entertainment site — Vue + Vite is the better choice.

The hybrid architecture adds complexity. Static pages and the runtime page use different rendering strategies, requiring understanding of two sets of logic.

Unresolved

If the game count exceeds 100, generateStaticParams full pre-generation becomes a bottleneck, requiring ISR or a Headless CMS — but that’s no longer zero-backend.

I didn’t dig deep into Vue’s prerendering solution. vite-plugin-prerender-staticsupports multi-route generation and SEO meta tags, which might be enough if the game count is small.

Astro is another direction worth watching. A developer built a 50+ game site with Astro + vanilla JS, keeping the JS bundle under 100KB gzip and emphasizing “each game only loads the JavaScript it actually needs.” This approach is in the same spirit as the facade pattern. If you’re in the selection phase, it’s worth half a day to look into.

What This Means for You

If you’re making a similar tech decision, here’s my advice:

Define your hard constraints first, then look at frameworks. If your constraints are the same as mine (SEO + first load + iframe not blocking the main thread), the real decision point isn’t “Next.js or Vue” — it’s “how to implement the facade pattern.” The framework is just a container. Pick one whose downsides you can live with.

Don’t just look at first-load JS size. The Vue version was 35KB smaller, but its LCP after prerendering was actually slower. The relationship between size and performance is more complex than a spec sheet suggests.

Building both versions for three days is more useful than reading thirty comparison articles. The point of this article isn’t to tell you to pick Next.js. It’s to show you how to reach your own conclusion.

Full Code

Both MVP versions are organized, including Next.js and Vue comparison branches. The test data comes from a local environment. If you get different results on real hardware, I’d love to hear about it.

This article is based on my own project’s selection notes. AI was used only for grammar checking and structural suggestions; the technical judgments and test data come from actual runs.

corrida_no_ar.titulo: CRIANÇA corre as DEZ MILHAS GAROTO de forma ILEGAL
corrida_no_ar.resumo: Criança corre 16 km ilegalmente, gerando debate sobre regras. Inscrições para a São Silvestre abrem hoje. Maratona de Boston anuncia corte rigoroso, NYRR impõe restrições em Nova York, e a espetacular mandala do Brasil Gigante, feita pela Metalvest, é revelada.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Quinta-feira | 1 de outubro de 2026

Um caso que gerou polêmica foi o de uma criança que correu as Dez Milhas Garoto, um percurso de 16 km, de forma ilegal. A criança participou da prova principal utilizando um número de peito da “Garotada”, a versão infantil do evento, que era para a corrida de 400 metros. O regulamento da prova infantil é claro, com distâncias adequadas para cada faixa etária: 200 metros (6-7 anos), 400 metros (8-9 anos), meia milha (10-13 anos) e uma milha (14-17 anos). O que aconteceu foi uma infração direta às regras da própria corrida e, mais importante, à Norma 12 da Confederação Brasileira de Atletismo (CBAt). Essa norma, atualizada em 3 de maio de 2026, estabelece as distâncias máximas permitidas em corridas de rua por faixa etária. Para correr 10 km, o atleta precisa ter no mínimo 16 anos. Para distâncias superiores, como os 16 km das Dez Milhas, é necessário estar na categoria Sub-20, ou seja, ter 18 ou 19 anos completos no ano da prova. O incidente levanta uma séria questão sobre a responsabilidade dos pais que, em vez de ensinarem o respeito às regras, incentivam os filhos a burlá-las desde cedo, colocando em risco a saúde da criança e dando um péssimo exemplo.

Inscrições abertas para a 101ª São Silvestre

As inscrições para a 101ª edição da Corrida Internacional de São Silvestre foram abertas para o público geral hoje, dia 30 de setembro, às 10h da manhã. Os interessados devem se inscrever exclusivamente pelo site oficial, saosilvestre.com.br, para evitar cair em golpes. A recomendação é fazer o pré-cadastro no novo sistema da Ticket Sports para agilizar o processo. A abertura tardia das inscrições, a apenas três meses da prova, é um ponto de crítica, pois dificulta o planejamento de corredores de fora de São Paulo que precisam comprar passagens e reservar hospedagem.

Maratona da Muralha 2027: edição comemorativa Down abre inscrições em breve

A Maratona da Muralha, uma das provas mais singulares do Brasil com apenas 42.195 metros de percurso e um número limitado de participantes, celebrará sua 10ª edição em 2027. Para comemorar, a prova será no formato “Down”, descendo de Visconde de Mauá para Penedo (RJ). As inscrições para este evento especial abrirão em um lote único no dia 6 de outubro de 2026, às 19:42:19, e costumam esgotar rapidamente. Atletas que participaram de todas as edições anteriores receberão um número de peito preto vitalício, que poderá ser passado para seus filhos.

Corte da Maratona de Boston 2027 deixa mais de 8 mil qualificados de fora

A organização da Maratona de Boston anunciou o tempo de corte para a edição de 2027. Para garantir a vaga, os corredores precisaram ser 5 minutos e 17 segundos mais rápidos que o tempo de qualificação exigido para sua respectiva faixa etária e gênero. Mesmo com um recorde de 25.630 atletas qualificados aceitos, a alta demanda deixou mais de 8.000 corredores que atingiram o índice, mas não o corte, fora da prova. Para esses atletas, haverá uma nova chance através de um sorteio de 1.000 vagas adicionais.

NYRR restringe ações de clubes e assessorias na Maratona de Nova York

A New York Road Runners (NYRR) anunciou novas restrições para as ações de clubes de corrida e assessorias durante a Maratona de Nova York. Em um comunicado, a organização proibiu o uso de itens como confetes, drones, giz no chão e o fornecimento de álcool nas “cheer zones”. Além disso, foi banida a exibição de marcas que não sejam patrocinadoras oficiais do evento. A medida visa organizar a festa popular que acontece ao longo do percurso, mas a fiscalização será um desafio, já que mais de um milhão de pessoas assistem à prova nas ruas.

Conheça a Metalvest, a empresa por trás da mandala do Brasil Gigante

A impressionante mandala do Circuito Brasil Gigante, uma medalha que, ao ser completada, pesa quase meio quilo, é produzida pela Metalvest. A empresa, que está há 30 anos no mercado, é especializada em criar medalhas e troféus de alta qualidade e com design diferenciado, sendo responsável por premiações de grandes eventos esportivos no Brasil, como as provas da Iguana Sports, o Troféu Brasil de Atletismo, o Campeonato Brasileiro de Jiu-Jitsu e muitas outras. Se você organiza um evento e quer uma premiação especial, vale a pena conhecer o trabalho deles.
